content: Bupivacaine, an amide local anesthetic, is available in two forms: hyperbaric and isobaric. These forms are administered intrathecally into the spinal canal to provide regional anesthesia for cesarean sections. Despite multiple clinical trials comparing the two forms, no conclusive evidence has been established to favor one over the other. This systematic review, initially published in 2013 and updated in 2016, aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of hyperbaric versus isobaric bupivacaine for spinal anesthesia in women undergoing cesarean sections. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared hyperbaric and isobaric bupivacaine in parturients undergoing elective cesarean sections. A total of 10 studies involving 614 participants were analyzed. Most trials were assessed as having an uncertain risk of bias in terms of randomization, but the overall risk of bias was considered low. However, the majority of the included trials had small sample sizes, which limited the strength of the conclusions. The primary outcome assessed was the need for conversion to general anesthesia. Across 10 trials, no significant difference was observed between the two groups in the rate of conversion to general anesthesia (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.33, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.09 to 1.17, very low-quality evidence). Similarly, nine trials found no significant difference in the need for supplemental analgesics (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.41, very low-quality evidence). Four trials comparing the requirement for ephedrine also showed no significant difference (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.38, very low-quality evidence). Adverse effects were also evaluated. Seven trials did not demonstrate a significant difference in the incidence of nausea and vomiting between the two groups (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.72, low-quality evidence). Three trials found no significant difference in the occurrence of post-dural puncture headache (Odds Ratio [OR] 1.82, 95% CI 0.47 to 6.99, low-quality evidence). Additionally, three trials showed no difference in the incidence of high spinal block (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.16 to 4.90). One notable finding was that hyperbaric bupivacaine resulted in a faster onset of sensory blockade at the thoracic 4th (T4) spinal level compared to isobaric bupivacaine. This was supported by two trials (Mean Difference [MD] -1.06 minutes, 95% CI -1.80 to -0.31, moderate-quality evidence). However, six trials found no significant difference in the total amount of ephedrine used (RR 0.23, 95% CI -1.65 to 2.12, moderate-quality evidence). The authors concluded that the overall quality of evidence for most outcomes was low or very low, primarily due to the limited data, small sample sizes, and suboptimal reporting in the included trials. While hyperbaric bupivacaine demonstrated a faster onset of sensory blockade at the T4 level, there was little evidence to suggest differences in the need for conversion to general anesthesia, supplemental analgesia, or adverse effects between the two forms. The rarity of these outcomes, variability in dosing, use of adjuvant drugs, and differences in regional anesthesia techniques likely contributed to the lack of significant findings. The review emphasized the need for larger, well-designed randomized trials to confirm any potential advantages of hyperbaric bupivacaine. Future research should also establish standardized and objective criteria for conversion to general anesthesia to ensure consistency across studies.
